title: Four Ministers Pledge a Coordination Center in the Philippines. Balikatan Already Tested One
dek: Japanese and Australian personnel took part in a coordination center at Camp Aguinaldo during this year’s Balikatan exercise, according to the Philippines’ then-military chief. What the Oct. 28 pledge would add, and has not yet described, is a center that four governments staff, govern and use outside exercises.

body_paragraphs.text: The defense ministers of Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States have committed to “establishing a Combined Coordination Center (CCC) in the Philippines.” The pledge heads a
joint statement on their Oct. 28 meeting in Cebu
, posted by Australia on Nov. 10 and
published in Japanese

by Japan’s Ministry of Defense the same day. Neither version says where the center will be, how it will be organized or when it will open; the Philippine Department of National Defense released it without further detail,
Manila Bulletin reported

. Yet a center by that name was inaugurated this year at Camp Aguinaldo, the headquarters of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) in Quezon City, and the Philippines’ former military chief has said it hosted
“elements from Japan and Australia”
during this year’s Balikatan exercise.
The center leads a list that also includes synchronized defense investments, closer policy consultations and expanded combined exercises. The idea was absent from the ministers’
Kuala Lumpur readout
of November 2025, and from Japan’s Oct. 28
readout
and Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro’s
news conference

, including its questions. Koizumi spoke instead of the acquisition and cross-servicing agreements (ACSAs) Japan holds with all three partners, and of working with Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. toward an agreement protecting classified military information.
The center began as a bilateral project. In November 2024, U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III and Teodoro
broke ground on a new combined coordination center at Camp Aguinaldo
during the visit on which the two countries signed a General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA). A
Department of Defense fact sheet
said it would improve bilateral operational planning and let the two forces work side by side on real-time incidents, “including those in the South China Sea.” In
Balikatan 24
and
Balikatan 25
, a CCC synchronized separate Philippine and U.S. joint task forces; a U.S. account of the latter called it “a secure, joint operations node” where each side kept running its own force.

Balikatan 2026 widened that node. At the exercise’s close on May 8, Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (INDOPACOM), said “the entire multinational force embedded this structure, including the newly inaugurated Combined Coordination Center,”
the INDOPACOM-sponsored Indo-Pacific Defense FORUM reported
The Philippine Daily Inquirer

reported that Paparo described it as a secure multinational command-and-control hub on encrypted allied networks, and that Gen. Romeo Brawner Jr., then the AFP chief of staff, said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had watched a live-fire drill through the center alongside military personnel from the United States, Australia, France, Canada, Japan and the Philippines. In
an edited FORUM interview published in September
, Brawner described “a common command center, or Combined Coordinating Center,” shared by U.S. and Philippine forces with elements from Japan and Australia.

Those accounts establish participation in an exercise, not standing membership. The claims about Japanese and Australian personnel rest on one Philippine officer, paraphrased in one report and recalled in an edited interview; Paparo’s remark supports multinational use only in general terms, and no Japanese or Australian government source reviewed here describes its personnel’s role. None says whether foreign officers hold billets there between exercises, under whose authority they served or what they could see. Nor was the exercise limited to the four: France and Canada were present, and
INDOPACOM said
its common operating picture reached eight nations.
This week’s accounts of the pledged center pull in different directions.
Manila Standard

described it on Nov. 12 as still a planned initiative. Asked about it on Nov. 11, Teodoro said, “There will be a coordination mechanism. Right now, it is already operating,” adding that locations could be disclosed once the parties agreed,
GMA News reported
The Inquirer noted
that he did not say whether the mechanism was the facility used in Balikatan or a separate arrangement.
Three readings fit that record: the Camp Aguinaldo center placed on a four-government footing; several sites in the Philippines, consistent with
USNI News’s report

of U.S.-funded centers throughout the country and Teodoro’s reference to locations; or a new body under a familiar name. As of Nov. 13, the statements and remarks reviewed here did not say which, so the exercise center and the pledged one are not established to be the same. Brawner’s
stated aim in May

of communication links to allied command centers in Japan, Australia and at INDOPACOM headquarters concerns connections abroad, not more sites. The four countries’ recently signed Pacific Chiefs of Defense Cooperation Council Terms of Reference, which
Manila Bulletin says
cover information sharing and planning interoperability, may hold part of the answer; their text was not reviewed.

If the pledge does mean a standing four-country center, what changes is less who takes part than on what terms. A standing center would mean officers from four militaries posted between exercises, each answering to a national chain of command. Command language runs through the May accounts, but the arrangement on the record is coordination of parallel national task forces,
as in Balikatan 25

, and the ministers’ statement speaks only of coordination. Paparo’s forecast of exercises led “through coalition combined command centers” is one commander’s description, not a four-government commitment. The legal ground cited is bilateral:
in Kuala Lumpur
the ministers applauded the Japan–Philippines Reciprocal Access Agreement’s entry into force, and
on Oct. 28
Koizumi spoke of turning it and the ACSAs into concrete unit operations. Australia’s arrangements with the Philippines are outside the sources reviewed.
Information is where a standing arrangement would have to do the most new work. The
GSOMIA the United States and the Philippines signed in 2024

covers classified military information shared between those two governments; Japan and the Philippines are still working toward an equivalent, Koizumi said on Oct. 28. During Balikatan the multinational picture ran
on a U.S. system

, with foreign disclosure officers tagging data to cross networks, so what a Japanese or Australian officer could see turned largely on U.S. release decisions. The sources reviewed here document no four-country instrument for classified information, a gap in the public record rather than proof that none exists.
The larger question is what the center would do between exercises. The 2024 fact sheet gave the bilateral center a role in real-time incidents, not only training, and
GMA reported

that exercise coordination had moved from the AFP Education and Training Command to Strategic Command, with Teodoro describing interoperability requirements as no longer limited to education and training. The statements do not say whether a four-country center would take on an incident role. Nor do they say who would pay: the record shows
only U.S. funding
for the Balikatan centers, and the investment pledge does not assign this one’s cost.

The record supports a narrower finding than the pledge’s wording invites. Japanese and Australian presence in a Philippine coordination center is not new; Balikatan 2026 showed it, alongside French and Canadian personnel, and the statement is silent on anyone beyond the four. What the ministers have committed to, without yet describing it, is the step from a center that hosts allies during an exercise to one that four governments maintain, with standing billets, an agreed basis for sharing classified information and a mandate that outlasts the exercise. That step would matter most if the new center inherits the 2024 center’s incident role, giving Japan and Australia a routine peacetime part in responses that include the South China Sea. Until the four say who is posted there, under what rules and for what tasks, the pledge reads as a commitment to make an exercise-tested arrangement permanent, not evidence that a standing four-country institution exists.

publisher_references.original_title: New mission network integrates allied, partner forces during Balikatan

verification.locator: May 15, 2026, by FORUM Staff. Classified official because FORUM is sponsored by USINDOPACOM and is not independent of the U.S. government (Laos Brief precedent for government-site sources), but it is a command-sponsored staff article, not an official command statement: the description of the center (at AFP headquarters, Camp Aguinaldo, a command and control hub between the AFP and USINDOPACOM for multinational coordination) is FORUM's. Adm. Samuel Paparo's words are direct quotes from the May 8, 2026 Balikatan closing ceremony in Manila and are attributed to him: 'The entire multinational force embedded this structure, including the newly inaugurated Combined Coordination Center'; future Balikatan exercises led from there '[Camp Aguinaldo]' (bracket is FORUM's) 'through coalition combined command centers'. Command naming: USINDOPACOM was restyled 'U.S. Pacific Command' as a secondary title from June 16, 2026 (pacom.mil release 'Department of War Restores U.S. Pacific Command Designation', seen in search excerpt); the Brief uses INDOPACOM for May 2026 events. Distinct from s18 (September 2026 FORUM interview).

verification.locator: Byline Gabryelle Dumalag, INQUIRER.net, 03:57 PM May 08, 2026 (article:published_time 2026-05-08T07:57Z). Balikatan 2026 closing ceremony and press briefing at Camp Aguinaldo. Section 'Triple C': 'the newly established Combined Coordination Center, also referred to as the "Triple C," inside Camp Aguinaldo'. Inquirer paraphrase, not quote: Paparo 'described the facility as a secure multinational command-and-control hub designed to coordinate multilateral operations and future Balikatan activities using encrypted communications networks shared among allies'; direct Paparo quote 'We've been working on this for five years. It's a reality.' Inquirer paraphrase of Brawner: Marcos 'monitored one of the recent live-fire drills in Ilocos through the center, alongside military personnel from the United States, Australia, France, Canada, Japan, and the Philippines'; goal 'to establish communication links with allied command centers outside the country, including those in Japan, Australia, and the US Indo-Pacific Command headquarters'. Squad chiefs to meet that afternoon on expanding Balikatan's area of operations via communications links, not troops abroad. Independent reporting of officials' statements; not evidence of standing billets. Retrieved 13 Nov 2026.

publisher_references.issuer: Indo-Pacific Defense Forum staff (USINDOPACOM-sponsored publication); interview with Gen. Romeo Brawner Jr.

verification.locator: Dated September 14, 2026, FORUM Staff; 'Correspondent Frances Mangosing contributed to this interview, which was edited to fit FORUM's format.' Brawner retired as AFP chief of staff in July 2026. Classified official on the s10 precedent (command-sponsored, not independent); the words are Brawner's, as edited by FORUM. Brawner: 'In the Balikatan 2026 exercise, we had not just the U.S. and the Philippines working together in a common command center, or Combined Coordinating Center, but we also had elements from Japan and Australia.' Stated plans, not facts: an AFP officer to be embedded in the U.S. Pacific Command ('We are just arranging the mechanics') and in Japan and Australia; 'we welcome these countries to be part of a command center, or control center, here in the Philippines.' The article uses 'U.S. Pacific Command' (post-June 2026 styling). Retrieved 13 Nov 2026.
